planting.note: Fall-sow seed directly on the soil surface so winter freeze-thaw cycles break dormancy, or set out container plants in spring into lean, rocky, well-drained clay or sandy soil typical of pinyon-juniper mesas; established plants resent summer irrigation.

directions: This Four Corners buckwheat forms a low rosette of woolly gray-green leaves from which reddish, wand-like flowering stems rise in mid to late summer, branching into loose clusters of small cream to pale pink flowers that age to rust red. It thrives on the same clay and gravelly soils that support pinyon-juniper woodland and is an important late-season nectar source after most spring wildflowers have finished. Avoid fertile garden soil or regular watering, both of which cause the plant to flop or rot; a gravel mulch over the crown helps it persist for years without irrigation. Leave old flowering stems standing through winter for seed-eating birds and over-wintering native bees.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into sandy or gravelly, sharply drained soil in full sun; this short-lived perennial self-sows readily once established and does not transplant well once its taproot forms, so avoid moving seedlings.

directions: Desert trumpet is instantly recognizable by the swollen, hollow sections along its otherwise wiry blue-green flowering stems, a trait unique among Colorado Plateau wildflowers and thought to help the plant conserve water. Tiny clusters of pale yellow flowers open atop the branched stems from late spring through fall, turning rust-colored as they set seed, and the dried, inflated stems persist as a sculptural accent through winter. Grow it in the leanest, rockiest spot in the garden alongside pinyon pine and juniper; rich soil or extra water produces lush but short-lived, floppy growth. It tolerates extreme heat and reflected sun from rock and gravel mulch better than almost any other native wildflower.

planting.note: Tuck rooted cuttings or small container divisions into vertical rock crevices, tufa, or a raised scree bed with almost no organic matter; wedge the roots into a crack so they stay cool and shaded while the foliage reaches for sun, mimicking its native sandstone cliff habitat.

directions: Rockmat is a true cliff-dweller of canyon country, rooting directly into cracks in sandstone and limestone faces across the Colorado Plateau, where it forms a flat, woody mat of small leathery gray-green leaves hugging the rock. Dense spike-like clusters of tiny white to cream flowers cover the mat in early to midsummer, drawing a steady stream of small native bees. In cultivation it is a specialty rock-garden plant best suited to a crevice garden, retaining wall, or scree bed with exceptional drainage, since it rots quickly in soil that stays wet. Once rooted into a crack it needs essentially no supplemental water or feeding and will slowly spread outward for decades.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or very early spring onto the surface of lean, mineral scree or clay-shale soil, since seed needs light and winter chill to germinate well; set container plants with the crown slightly raised to shed water and prevent rot.

directions: Hoary townsendia forms a tight silver-haired cushion of narrow leaves on clay and shale slopes within pinyon-juniper and sagebrush country, nearly disappearing beneath its own flowers each spring. Large pink to lavender daisy-like blooms open almost stemless directly from the foliage in April and May, far out of proportion to the plant's small size, then fade as the cushion rests through summer heat. It is a favorite of rock gardeners for edging troughs, crevice gardens, and scree beds where its need for brutal drainage can be met; wet feet in winter are its single biggest threat. Established plants are extremely long-lived and drought-tolerant, needing no water beyond natural precipitation once their roots reach into the gravel below.

planting.note: Fall-sow seed directly into sharply drained sandy or rocky soil so it receives natural winter cold-moist stratification; or set out small container plants in early spring on a slickrock-style scree bed with the crown kept proud of standing water.

directions: Newberry's twinpod grows wedged into sandstone ledges and crevices across the slickrock canyon country of southern Utah and northern Arizona, forming a low cushion of rounded, felted gray-green leaves. In early spring it produces dense clusters of bright yellow four-petaled flowers directly above the foliage, followed by the distinctive inflated, two-chambered seed pods that give the genus its common name. It is grown by rock-garden and xeriscape specialists in crevice gardens or raised scree beds that replicate its native sandstone habitat, since any soil that holds moisture around the crown will rot it within a season. Once established on sharply drained gravel it needs no irrigation beyond natural rainfall and tolerates extreme summer heat and winter cold with equal ease.

planting.note: Fall-sow cleaned seed directly outdoors to satisfy its long cold-moist stratification requirement, or plant container or bare-root stock in fall in a canyon-bottom or foothill setting with rocky but slightly deeper soil than its upland pinyon-juniper neighbors prefer.

directions: Fendler's barberry is a thin-leaved, deciduous shrub of canyons and foothill thickets across the Four Corners region, forming an arching, loosely branched mound quite different from the stiff evergreen hollies many gardeners picture when they hear barberry. Small pale yellow flowers in spring give way to bright red, translucent, tart berries by late summer that persist into fall and are readily eaten by birds, while the foliage turns soft yellow to orange before dropping. It prefers the slightly cooler, less baked microsites found at canyon mouths and along intermittent drainages within pinyon-juniper woodland, tolerating part shade better than most companions on this list. Once established it needs only occasional deep watering during the driest months and otherwise shrugs off drought, heat, and cold with little care.
